result.summary: Our patch adds the textbook CWE-022 defense-of-record — canonicalize the base and the resolved file, then verify the file stays inside the base directory (with a correct `startsWith(base + separator)` boundary check) — placed at FileResourceManager.getResource, which is the single convergence point of every taint trace (all four end at `new File(base, path)` line 89-90). This neutralizes the whole traversal class (`../`, Windows `\`, and symlink escapes) at the sink rather than blocking one payload. It reaches the vulnerability by a different, valid mechanism/location than the official fix (which normalizes/blocks the OS separator up in the request handlers), and is arguably stronger. Main caveats: execution evidence is weak (POV did not reproduce pre-patch, 0 regressions run), the check only covers FileResourceManager (not other ResourceManager implementations), and canonicalization may over-restrict legitimate in-base symlinks pointing outside.
result.root_cause: Tainted request path flows into `new File(base, path)` in FileResourceManager.getResource without verifying the resolved file remains within the base directory, letting crafted separators/`..` escape the web root.

dimensions.rationale: Canonical-path containment at the sink makes FileResourceManager provably reject any resolved path outside base, closing the class not just the payload.

issues.description: Execution evidence is weak: POV did not reproduce before the patch and 0 regression tests ran, so real-world elimination is inferred from code reasoning, not demonstrated.
Check only protects FileResourceManager; requests served through other ResourceManager implementations retain no sink-level containment guard.

getCanonicalPath resolves symlinks, so a legitimate symlink inside base that targets an out-of-base location would be rejected (possible over-restriction), and canonicalization adds filesystem I/O per request.
